profiles.meeting_scenario: At a Dutch teaching hospital, a troubleshooting meeting has been called after the internal quality board noticed that the hospital's own review of serious adverse events seems to undercount diagnostic follow-up failures compared with patterns reported in a national retrospective analysis of 109 Dutch diagnostic SAE reports. The immediate trigger is a recent cluster of cases in which abnormal imaging or lab results were documented but not acted on quickly enough, yet local reviewers categorized several of them as 'communication issues' rather than 'diagnostic errors.' The meeting brings together the physician lead for diagnostic safety and the clinical informatics lead to diagnose why the hospital's incident-review process is not reliably surfacing these cases. The agenda is to examine where the review workflow breaks down, identify the root cause of the apparent undercount, and agree on a practical fix for the next quarterly SAE audit cycle. The expected outcome is a shared plan to 'tighten follow-up review' and 'close the loop on results,' although each participant silently imagines a different implementation and endpoint.

members.name: Dr. Eva van Loon
members.role: Internal Medicine Consultant and Diagnostic Safety Lead
members.expertise: Diagnostic error review, serious adverse event committee work, inpatient clinical reasoning, cross-specialty case analysis
members.background: Eva is an internist who chairs the hospital's diagnostic safety subgroup and has participated in regional patient-safety collaborations using DEER-style phase analysis for retrospective case reviews. She is accustomed to reading narrative SAE reports and interviewing clinicians to reconstruct where diagnostic assessment or follow-up broke down.
members.private_state: She wants the next audit cycle to show that the hospital is identifying diagnostic follow-up failures more accurately without creating a large new operational burden for physicians. She is also concerned that the current coding process obscures clinically important missed opportunities because reviewers rely too heavily on documented message transmission rather than on whether anyone integrated the result into the diagnostic picture.
hidden_assumptions: If a test result is abnormal and no clinician meaningfully integrates it into the working diagnosis or plan, the 'follow-up' failed even if the result was technically delivered in the EHR.

When people say they need to 'close the loop,' they mean confirming that a responsible clinician recognized the significance of the result and initiated or documented an appropriate next diagnostic step.
The relevant 'review period' for a diagnostic SAE extends across handoffs and shortly after discharge if the unresolved inpatient finding should reasonably have triggered action.
A practical 'fix' for the review process means changing the committee's case reconstruction and coding prompts so latent diagnostic follow-up failures become visible during retrospective analysis.

members.name: Jeroen Smit
members.role: Clinical Informatics Pharmacist and EHR Results Management Lead
members.expertise: EHR inbox workflows, result-routing logic, alert configuration, incident trend analysis, protocol implementation
members.background: Jeroen is a pharmacist by training who now leads hospital-wide optimization of results management in the electronic health record. He routinely works with incident reports involving unacknowledged test results, routing errors, and task queues, and he translates safety concerns into system changes and protocol updates.
members.private_state: He wants to contain the problem to a tractable workflow issue that can be solved through routing rules, acknowledgment tracking, and standard operating procedures rather than opening a broader debate about clinicians' diagnostic reasoning. He is worried that if the issue is framed too broadly, the informatics team will be tasked with fixing something impossible to measure.
hidden_assumptions: If the correct inbox received the result and someone acknowledged it within the configured timeframe, then the communication chain is intact; any later missed diagnosis is no longer a results-management problem.
When people say they need to 'close the loop,' they mean ensuring the result was routed, viewed, and marked acknowledged by the assigned team according to policy.
The relevant 'review period' for troubleshooting this problem ends when the inpatient team's ownership ends; outpatient or post-discharge actions belong to a separate follow-up process.
A practical 'fix' means adding or tightening technical controls in the EHR and protocol language so result ownership and acknowledgment are auditable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the hospital needs to 'close the loop on abnormal results.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means that a clinician must recognize the result's diagnostic significance and translate it into an appropriate next assessment, escalation, or documented plan.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means that the EHR must show successful routing, viewing, and acknowledgment of the result by the responsible team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard patient-safety language and sounds obviously shared; both see acknowledgment and action as related, so neither expects the other to be using a narrower versus broader definition.

misalignment_points.topic: Which cases count as follow-up failures
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'follow-up errors' as the category that seems undercounted in local SAE review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts a case as a follow-up error when a result was available but no adequate diagnostic response occurred within a clinically reasonable window, including after discharge if the inpatient episode created the obligation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts a case as a follow-up error only when the result was not routed, not seen, or not acknowledged according to workflow rules during the inpatient ownership period.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are not arguing about whether follow-up matters; they silently apply different thresholds for what qualifies, and because both examples involve delayed action after testing, the category label feels sufficient.

misalignment_points.topic: What period the review should cover
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the review should track the case 'through follow-up' before the next quarterly audit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes 'through follow-up' includes handoffs to another ward, weekend cross-cover, discharge instructions, and whether pending results generated action in the first days after discharge.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes 'through follow-up' means through the inpatient results-management chain until the assigned team's task queue is completed or ownership is transferred in the system.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In troubleshooting discussions, 'follow-up' naturally sounds like a shared end-to-end concept, but each person's routine work defines the boundary differently and neither sees that boundary as a negotiable meeting topic.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'tighten the review prompts' for the next SAE audit cycle.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to revise committee interview guides and case-review templates so reviewers ask whether abnormal findings changed the differential diagnosis, whether contingency plans existed, and where cognitive or coordination breakdowns occurred.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to add structured fields and audit checks in the incident-review form tied to result-routing timestamps, acknowledgment status, and documented owner assignment.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The action sounds like a minor process refinement rather than a strategic choice, and both approaches plausibly fit under 'review prompts,' so surface agreement persists despite different execution plans.

turns.inner_thought: The quality board is right: we are probably missing diagnostic follow-up failures because reviewers stop at whether a result was documented or transmitted. In the Dutch SAE analyses, the real issue was often that no one actually incorporated the abnormal finding into the evolving diagnostic picture. If we keep coding these as generic communication issues, the next audit cycle will again understate the problem and we will learn nothing useful.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What worries me is that our recent SAE reviews seem to be missing the same kinds of problems highlighted in the Dutch retrospective analysis. We keep seeing cases with delayed action after an abnormal finding, but locally they don't always end up counted as follow-up errors. I'd like us to understand where that drift is happening in the review process.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, most of these incidents are still results-management problems: routing, inboxes, ownership, acknowledgment. I do not want this to become an open-ended debate about clinical reasoning, because then informatics gets handed an unmeasurable safety problem. If we define the task as closing the loop on abnormal results, I can translate that into auditable workflow controls.
turns.utterance: Yes, I see the same signal, although from the informatics side most of the flagged files still look like results-management issues. To me the immediate goal should be to close the loop on abnormal results more reliably, because if that part is inconsistent the review will always look messy.

turns.inner_thought: Take that CT abdomen case: the report raised possible ischemia, but nobody broadened the differential, escalated, or made a meaningful plan. That is exactly the kind of follow-up failure I want visible. If we label it only as communication, we erase the missed diagnostic opportunity.
turns.utterance: A good example is that CT abdomen case from last month. The report raised a serious possibility, and yet the case review still read more like a communication lapse than a follow-up error. For me that's exactly the sort of case where we should be asking whether we actually closed the loop on an abnormal result.

turns.inner_thought: In that CT case, radiology routed the result correctly, the medicine team received it, and someone acknowledged it within the policy window. So as a results-management issue, the loop was closed. Whatever went wrong after that belongs downstream, not in the communication chain. I need to keep that boundary intact.
turns.utterance: I know the case you mean. What makes it tricky is that, on paper, the result did reach the medicine team and it was acknowledged within policy. So in that sense the loop was closed, and the breakdown appears later than the point where we usually classify a follow-up error.

turns.inner_thought: He is still anchoring on receipt and acknowledgment. But if we want the committee to detect the real failure, the review period has to extend across handoffs and immediately after discharge when unresolved inpatient findings still need action. Otherwise the very cases we're worried about fall outside the frame.
turns.utterance: That may be part of the problem. I think the review needs to track the case through follow-up rather than stopping at the first documented handoff point. In several of these files, what mattered happened over a transition or just after discharge, and if we don't look there we will keep undercounting.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with tracking through follow-up, but for me that means following the ownership chain until the inpatient queue is completed or transferred correctly. That is the tractable part: who owned the result, whether the queue was cleared, and whether discharge left anything unresolved in the system. I can support that without drifting into post-discharge diagnostic judgment.
turns.utterance: I agree that we should track it through follow-up. We probably need a clearer view of what happens at handoff, whether ownership is explicit, and whether things are actually completed before the inpatient episode is closed. If that part is visible, the review should become more consistent.

turns.inner_thought: The committee is coding from the artifact trail instead of reconstructing the diagnostic pathway. A sent message is not the same as follow-up. If the abnormal result never changed the assessment or plan, then the failure is being hidden by our current prompts.
turns.utterance: Exactly. My concern is that reviewers are leaning too heavily on whether a message was sent or noted, instead of asking whether the finding actually changed the assessment or triggered a plan. That's where I think some of these follow-up errors are disappearing from sight.

turns.inner_thought: If we tighten the review prompts, I want structured checks: assigned owner, routing path, acknowledgment timing, weekend delays, exceptions. Those are data elements we can audit and compare. That gives us a practical fix without expanding into subjective review of reasoning.
turns.utterance: Then one practical step would be to tighten the review prompts for the next cycle. Right now the form doesn't force people to capture some basic checkpoints consistently, and that makes the committee's coding too dependent on free text.

turns.inner_thought: Good, but the prompts have to ask about the working diagnosis, what changed after the result, and whether there was any contingency planning. Otherwise we'll just get a cleaner version of the same blind spot. If I can get those questions into the review template and interview guide, the hidden missed opportunities will start to surface.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree we should tighten the review prompts. I'd also like the reviewers to be more explicit in how they reconstruct the case, so we're not just recording that a result existed but also whether the clinical picture and next steps were made clear in the file.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot on ten SAE files is manageable. Once the structured checks are in place, we can count how many follow-up errors are identified under a more standardized process. Ideally that will show the issue is mainly around auditable workflow variance, which is something my team can address.
turns.utterance: Why don't we pilot the fix on the next ten SAE files? If we tighten the review prompts and apply them the same way each time, we can compare how many follow-up errors are detected before the quarterly audit and see whether consistency improves.

turns.inner_thought: That works, as long as the pilot really follows cases across the vulnerable period and not just to inbox completion. I want the delayed imaging and lab cases used as anchors so the committee starts seeing what a missed follow-up opportunity looks like in practice. If we say we're tightening follow-up review and closing the loop, everyone will assume the right thing.
turns.utterance: That sounds sensible. So we'll tighten follow-up review before the next quarterly audit and use the recent delayed-result cases as worked examples. If we do that well, we should be in a better position to close the loop on results and understand why these cases are being classified the way they are.

turns.inner_thought: I'll draft a review sheet with the fields I need and pull the routing and acknowledgment data from the EHR. That should let us show whether the revised process makes follow-up error detection more consistent without committing to a broad diagnostic-reasoning overhaul.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll draft the updated review sheet and pull the relevant EHR data so we have something concrete to test against the files. Then we can see whether the new process improves consistency in how these cases are reviewed.
